speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT-EMMA WOIKIN-PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF SENATOR HORNER
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege. It has reference to a statement which is alleged to have been made by Senator Ralph Horner and which appeared in the Ottawa Evening Journal of April 2. The article is headed, "Western senator recommended Emma Woikin," and the first paragraph reads:
Mrs. Emma Woikin, one of the twelve temporary civil servants charged as a suspect in the investigation of the Russian spy network, was recommended for a government job by Senator Ralph Horner.
"Yes," the Progressive Conservative senator from Blaine Lake, Saskatchewan, to-day told the Evening Journal, "I recommended Emma Woikin-but for the char service-not as a cipher clerk in the code room of the external affairs department."
The senator, a big, bluff and frankly-spoken man, has been "a little annoyed" at the way things have worked out.
The paragraph to which I wish to refer to particularly is as follows:
"The only reason Emma Woikin found her way into a stenographic position, first at the passport office and then in the cipher division of external affairs," said the senator, "was because her father and brothers year after year have voted Liberal for Mr. Mackenzie King."
I asked the under-secretary of state for external affairs if he would give me a statement as to how Mrs. Woikin came to be employed in the Department of External Affairs, and I have the following from Mr. Robertson:
Due to the pressure of work in the passport office in the autumn of 1943. the Department of External Affairs, on September 8, 1943, requisitioned the civil service commission for three additonal clerks grade 2 and two typists grade
2.	At the same time, treasury board was requested to establish temporary positions to take care of the new appointees. On September 10, 1943, Mrs. Emma Woikin, who was classified as a typist, grade 1, was assigned by the civil service commission to one of the new temporary posts as no grade 2 typist was then available.
That is the official statement on the matter. I might add that until I heard the name of Mrs. Woikin mentioned in connection with *>
the investigation now proceeding I had no knowledge of there being any person of that name, either in Prince Albert constituency or in the public service of Canada. Unlike Senator Horner I neither recommended Mrs. Woikin for a government job nor was I
Travel Abroad

requested by her or by anyone to make a recommendation on her behalf. I know nothing whatever about her appointment; it was entirely a civil service matter and procedure.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PRESS REPORTS REFERRING TO SPEECH OF MR. KNOWLES ON MARCH 19
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege which has to do with a newspaper report making reference to a speech which I made in this House of Commons on March 19. The report appeared in yesterday's Winnipeg daily newspapers; as a matter of fact it is exactly the same in both the Free Press and the Tribune. It reports a political meeting held on Monday night at which Mr. David Graham charged, on the basis of the speech which I made on March 19, that when I was in Moscow recently I failed to present the Canadian viewpoint to the Russian people whom I met, and that I failed to assure them that they need have no fear of our western democracies. It is stated also that I had urged friendship for their spy activities and that my advocacy of understanding was a one-way proposition.
I rise to this question of privilege because it is statements of this kind that make it difficult to establish the type of relationship which we all want between yds country and the Soviet Union, and also because the facts are the very opposite of the statements made by Mr. Graliam. Not only did I in my speech urge various efforts such as the publishing in Moscow of a Canadian paper in Russian so as to interpret Canadian ways to these people, but when I was there I made the same kind of appeal I am now making here. I am now seeking to persuade the Canadian people to understand the Russians. Similarly when I was in Moscow I went to a great deal of effort to try to get the people with whom I was in conversation to understand our ways and to realize that what we really want is friendship. I shall continue my effort to achieve understanding and friendship on a mutual basis.

maintopic: TRAVEL ABROAD ABOLITION OF EXIT PERMITS-CONDITIONS AFFECTING PASSPORT CONTROL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: TRAVEL ABROAD ABOLITION OF EXIT PERMITS-CONDITIONS AFFECTING PASSPORT CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to table order in council P.C. 1272, April 2, 1946, revoking order in council P.C. 1841 of March 10, 1942, as amended, concerning the issuance of exit permits to women, and children under the age of sixteen years, proceeding to destinations outside the western hemisphere.
I should like to say something about the order in council which I have just tabled. It removes a form of travel restriction which has been in existence since March 10, 1942. Under the regulation that was introduced at that time, and which has been amended on several occasions since, the movement of women, and children under the age of sixteen, to destinations outside the western hemisphere has been limited by the necessity of their securing an exit permit before being permitted to leave Canada. As I mentioned on Friday last, the government is anxious to relax war-time controls wherever possible, and in view of the gradual improvement in travel conditions it has been decided to abolish the requirement of an exit permit immediately.
The result of the present order in council is that, subject to the existing rules of passport control exercised by the Department of External Affairs, women and children residing in Canada are free to make their own travel arrangements without first obtaining an exit permit from the immigration branch of the Department of Mines and Resources.
I wish, however, to emphasize that, although the improvement on general travel conditions has made it possible to remove the exit permit restrictions, this step should not be taken as an indication that the strain on transportation facilities to Europe and the far east has ceased to exist. Moreover, as the Minister of Mines and Resources mentioned in his statement on Monday last, there are severe difficulties in connection with travel from Europe to this country, and these necessarily affect any plans for travel from Canada that involve a later return trip back to Canada. The transportation of Canadian servicemen and their dependents from the United Kingdom and the continent to this country is

Atomic Energy
being granted the highest priority in the allocation of west-bound shipping space. This movement will require a very large .percentage of available passenger accommodation for many months to come, and the government desires to warn persons intending to travel to the United Kingdom and Europe during 1946 that no assurance can be given of return transportation until the needs of the repatriation programme have been filled. It is further pointed out that a very large waiting list has developed in the United Kingdom of persons who are not at present eligible for westbound shipping passage. These applicants, which number in the thousands, will be accommodated first, and temporary visitors to the United Kingdom and the continent will of course be required to take their places on the waiting list. As far as can be foreseen, this will unfortunately involve very long delays.
So far as passport control is concerned, I have already mentioned that certain types of administrative control on .passport endorsements are being exercised by the Department of External Affairs. These have been necessitated by the limited housing, food and transportation facilities in Europe and the far east, and by the desire of the government to restrict non-essential movement from Canada to the countries where conditions are particularly serious as a result of the war. The past few months have been marked by a gradual improvement in these conditions, and I am able to state that the question of passport control is at present under review.

In view of the fact that Canada is one of the three partners in the development of atomic energy, and that the United States has made provision for 120 senators and congressmen to attend Operation Crossroad at Bikini Atoll, will the Prime Minister tell the house how many Canadian senators and members of parliament will be sent to represent Canada's interest?
The answer is: I understand that the United States government had invited a small congressional committee of less than ten senators and congressmen to attend the operation which
it was proposed to have held at Bikini Atoll. As the hon. member knows, this operation has been postponed sine die. speechtext:
Mr. W. R.' THATCHER (MoOse Jaw) moved:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the advisability of instituting a reasonable immigration programme, planned in accordance with Canada's absorptive capacity, its economic needs and possibilities of development.
He said:	In introducing this resolution on
immigration, I do so with the knowledge that, perhaps no single issue in Canada to-day is fraught with so much emotional thinking and prejudice.
Notwithstanding this, the fact remains that to-day thousands of Europeans are knocking at Canada's door, eager to make new homes in this country. These people are not castoffs or failures; many are the best their respective countries have to offer. Among them are men who fought long and gallantly for the allied cause during the recent war. This parliament must decide, and decide soon, whether it is in the national interest to admit into Canada a number of these people, or whether it is in the national interest to maintain our present immigration laws.
Whatever the view of hon. members may be, there is no denying the fact that immigration has been the life-history of this nation. There

Immigration
are few Canadians who do not trace back their ancestry to at least one nation of the old world. In this very House of Commons thirty-four members originally were European immigrants.
You will note that the resolution before the house is framed in a very general way. It asks the government to consider "the advisability of instituting a reasonable immigration programme." I hope that that wording will not give offence to hon. members on either side of the house.
Suppose we look for a moment at Canada's present immigration policy. Very few realize how extremely restrictive that policy is. Dating back to 1930, it is based largely on the economic fears and errors of the great depression. The policy was founded on the hopelessness and lack of faith in the country's future wrhich was prevalent during the nineteen thirties. All immigrants other than British and American subjects, with a few minor exceptions, are virtually excluded. In the five year period 1940 to 1944 an average of less than 10,000 immigrants were allowed to enter Canada annually.
In my opinion there are three main weaknesses in our present immigration policy. First it is based on racial discrimination and outworn prejudices. The law sets up several preferred and non-preferred groups. Britons and Americans are included in the preferred category, and also in the select group are the citizens of such nations as France, Belgium, Holland, Germany, the Scandinavian countries, and one or two others. The law places in the nonpreferred category those who come from Poland, the Ukraine, Austria, Czechoslovakia and a few other countries. In a final category are placed those who come from Turkey, Roumania, Greece, Italy and those who are of Jewish nationality. Those people can get into the country only by special permit. It seems strange that during the recent war, at the very time Canadians were being urged to enlist to help in eradicating racial intolerance abroad, our own nation was practising similar intolerance at home in selecting its immigrants. Surely it is more sensible to pick out immigrants for their skills, for their trades, for their physical backgrounds, than to take them for their race. For instance, it is quite conceivable that a central European, a hardy sturdy peasant born on the soil or, say a Finlander, an experienced logger, would make a better immigrant that a slum dweller from some city in iEngland. I believe, therefore,
that the first weakness of our immigration policy is that our immigrants are picked primarily for their race.
In the second place, it is very difficult to justify our present, immigration policy on purely humanitarian grounds. The war in Europe resulted in millions of people being uprooted and scattered far and wide. Many of. them cannot return to their old homes, and most of them are living in albject poverty. There is widespread lack of shelter and clothing. Food is so scarce that thousands of them are dying of malnutrition. Confiscation of property has been fairly general throughout many European countries. Certainly racial and religious prejudices prevail at every hand. Hundreds of .thousands of orphans are homeless in Europe.
Will you permit me, Mr. Speaker, to quote from a letter written by W. Wanka, a Sudeten German who emigrated to Canada in 1039:
In 1939 Canada opened her gates to 1,000 Sudetans. They settled on the land and found happiness in this great country. The mere fact that we are here to-day has kept many of our friends and relatives still in Europe from succumbing to black despair during the misery of the past months. The hopes of many thousands of anti-nazi Sudetens are centred upon us. Hardly a letter reaches us in which we are not asked to voice their plight, and to ask Canada anew for homes for them.
Many of those who are suffering to-day are former allies. The vast majority of these refugees were active opponents or victims of the fascist countries. The condition of these people, which is beyond description, pleads for them. Canada, in the interests of justice and humanity,_ cannot indefinitely ignore that plea.
In the third place, I believe that our immigration policy is contrary to the interests of the nation as a whole. No thoughtful person can travel across Canada without a feeling that there is an immense area whose economic resources have not yet been properly exploited. The general process, of settlement has been neither complete nor satisfactory. A moderate, well-planned immigration policy would have numerous advantages for Canadians generally In the first place, the larger population, by increasing the home market, would aid the economic stabilization of our economy. To-day, to a considerable degree, the prosperity of Canada is dependent upon our foreign export markets. If these foreign markets are good, generally speaking Canada is prosperous. If these foreign markets are bad, usually the opposite is true.
In other words, the economic well-being of Canada to-day is dependent to a large degree on conditions over which we have no control. This is particularly true of our agriculture.
Immigration

The largest .proportion of our wheat, hogs, cattle and other products are, I believe, shipped overseas. However, it is also true of our manufacturing industries. During the war our manufacturing capacity, I am told, was increased by thirty to forty per cent. If in the future we are to avoid idle factories and unemployment, if this greater plant capacity is to be fully utilized, we must do one of two things: either we must find a greater sxport market, or we must increase our home market. Immigration would permit Canada to increase her home market, thus curtailing our dependence on unstable foreign markets.
In the second place, immigration would ease the tax burden of Canadians. It was believed at one time that Canada would have a population several times its present twelve million people. Our provincial government buildings, with their large staffs and very large overhead, were set up with that thought in mind. Our railroad development also has had as its objective the serving of a population several times as large as twelve million. Additional people are needed to carry the heavy financial load which we have taken up. Our taxation burden could be eased by spreading it over a larger number of people.	«
In the third place, under certain circumstances it is probable that immigration would actually increase employment in Canada. All immigrants need new homes, furniture and other necessities of life. If they are going on a farm they need farm machinery, equipment and tools. Manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers and labourers would all benefit by this new business.
A further direct reaction would be to increase railway freight and railway passenger traffic, and I think it is quite probable that the railroads would have to take on additional employees if we had an immigration policy. Moreover, where the immigrant is one who is likely to invest capital, or who has some special and needed skill, he is likely to enhance the employment of Canadians. For instance, I am particularly mindful of a Czech refugee who moved to Saskatoon around 1938. He left Czechoslovakia just ahead of Hitler's occupation of that country. He had been a butcher in Poland. When he reached Saskatoon he found an empty factory building, where he m proceeded to set himself up in the meatpacking business. To-day that refugee employs about 600 men and women. The immigrant, unless he comes to some unproductive employment, creates additional work for the people already .in the community and adds to the general wealth of that community.

In the fourth place, immigrants bring to the nation new aptitudes, new skills and new scientific knowledge. Let us not forget that in centuries past the Flemish weavers, the Huguenots, and others brought new skills and a new outlook to Great Britain and helped to a considerable degree to make the empire industrially what she is to-day. Canada should benefit similarly from the gradual enrichment that comes from fresh streams of newcomers. For example, it is a well known fact that during the latter years of the recent war, immigrant scientists in the United States played a tremendous part in helping to split the atom and in making the atomic bomb. Who can say how the course of history would have been affected had the United States refused, to accept those immigrants at that time? I have heard it said1-it may be incorrect but I have heard the statement made

that some of these very scientists who went to the United States tried to get into Canada and could not do so because of our immigration laws. I suggest therefore that immigration will bring new skills and new aptitudes to the country which will prove very valuable to us.
Finally, I believe that Canada needs a larger population for purely defensive reasons. In this land-hungry world, twelve million people cannot hold half a continent indefinitely. I believe our poorly filled dominion is a danger to peace. We are asking for trouble if we refuse to take elementary precautions to increase our population in proportion to the nation's absorptive capacity. If we steadily refuse to take steps to populate our country, we may find in the future that some other nation will step in and do it for us.
In the past, most opposition to immigration has come from organized labour. This feeling was based largely on the premise that immigrants would deprive Canadians of work. Conceivably this view might be justified if there were only a limited and defined amount of work in the country, which could be divided among the people. However, most labour leaders have now accepted the belief that immigration by itself produces new wealth, creates demands for manufactured goods and services, and acts generally as an aid to trade, business, and employment.
Many immigrants bring capital and business experience with them, and become employers of labour rather than employees. There are also some immigrants who are willing to take jobs for which enough native applicants cannot be found. These classes certainly do not "take away jobs from Canadians." Moreover, a large number of immigrants are not wage earners and hence are not com-

Immigration
peti'tors. Among these are people too old to work, women who remain housewives, and young children.
The economic and social maladjustments to which our attention is drawn by the immigration issue are for the most part problems which are fundamental to our present society, whether or not immigration is involved. For instance, in the United States the problems associated with poverty, illiteracy and so forth are nowhere more apparent than in the southeastern cotton belt, a region where there has been the least immigration in past years.
It is interesting to note that at its 1944 convention the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada passed the following resolution:
Be it resolved that Canada's Immigration Act be revised to make it possible for Canada to do her share in granting refuge to her full quota of refugees.	,	,
Be it further resolved that a policy of accepting immigrants into this country be proceeded with as long as such policy in no way adversely affects living standards or the welfare of our present Canadian population.
The Canadian Congress of Labour passed a similar resolution at its convention in 1944, which reads as follows:
Be it'resolved that the C.C.L. in convention assembled request the dominion government to institute a concrete plan of immigration during the post-war period, without any danger of displacement of present labour.
In passing, it is interesting to note the steps that other nations have taken recently with regard to immigration. Crowded England has admitted some two hundred thousand refugees during and since the war. The United States has admitted thousands, and plans to bring in many more. Australia recently announced plans to absorb seventy thousand adults and seventeen thousand children a year. France is actively encouraging immigration. Canada, one of the most lightly populated areas in the world, appears to lag behind.
In conclusion may I say that I am not advocating a policy of wide-open immigration, nor would I support such a proposal. Rather I am asking the government to enunciate a moderate, well-planned immigration policy based on Canada's absorptive capacity and her moral responsibilities to the united nations organization.
It seems to me that the programme should be a flexible one, taking into consideration from year to year the labour needs of the nation. Moreover, I believe that immigrants should be picked not on a basis of race, but for their skills and for their physical backgrounds. Above all else, the policy must in no way be allowed to affect adversely the welfare of our present population. To-day the lives and liberties of millions throughout
the world are in danger. Canada, in keeping with her traditions, must bear a share of this great human problem. A great opportunity for our nation is at hand. I do not think that we should delay in taking advantage of it.

May I join with the hon. member who has just spoken on this question and say that he has presented the problem not only fairly but capably. I, too, do not advocate an open-door policy, but I do advocate immigration. I have here a few figures which I think would be interesting to the house. There are few people who know that the area of Canada is three and a half million square miles or fifty per cent larger than continental Europe, which is
2.116.000	square miles in area. While Europe supports four hundred million people we have approximately twelve million people. It might also be interesting to note that the unoccupied agricultural land of Canada amounts to
293.000	square miles, or 80.000 square miles more than the area occupied at the present time. As I- have just said, the population of Canada is approximately twelve millions with a distribution of 3-7 inhabitants per square mile as compared with Belgium with 802 inhabitants per square mile.
Most hon. members have read the report recently issued by the dominion bureau of statistics. This report, based on present trends, states that the population of Canada is likely to reach fifteen millions in 1990. The planning and development of Canada from confederation on were based on continually expanding population. Since the first world war it has become evident that the trends have been other than what were expected. There were three reasons for that. The first was the heavy emigration to the United States; the second was the smallet Canadian families, and the third was the sharp decline in immigration from Europe. The first two factors were outside the scope of the government because they were governed by social and economic forces; but the third factor was the result of a positive act carried out by the government. The door was closed. It is more important to-day than it has ever been to examine the problem and survey present conditions on both sides of the door. N
I have a few more statistics which I should like to give to the house. At confederation the population of this country was 2,700,000. Then came the Sifton immigration policy from 1896 to 1911, and it brought 3,000,000 immigrants into Canada. In 1906 the number was 211,653; in 1907, 272,409; in 1910, 286,839, and in 1911, 33,288. From 1911 to 1930 we averaged 100,000 annually, but there were two
Immigration

high years. In 1912 we brought in 375,756, and in 1913, 400,870. In one year we brought in only 41,000. In 1931 we brought in 27,500, and in 1935, 11,000. During other years immigration was negligible.
Canada must take cognizance of its changed economy. We have become a great industrial country, but can we afford to neglect our agricultural classes? To-day the farmers are begging for labour. We cannot constantly rely upon German prisoners of war and conscientious objectors to pull us out of the hole.

The difficulty with that resolution of my own party is that it is open to the same criticism as are the remarks of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) and of the mover of the resolution. It deals in generalities. It expresses hope, and I will be frank and say that I am not in position to improve very much upon what has been said by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, by the hon. member for Spadina, and by this resolution.
Let us be -practical about this thing. Consideration, yes; and I have no doubt that when the minister stands up he will tell us that they are giving it active consideration. But let me say this. Those of us who speak of the broad policy of immigration must be completely forgetful of our housing conditions. Anyone who suggests that at this moment we should bring into this country any number of persons is surely forgetful of the fact that at the moment we are unable to house our own people, particularly those who have returned to us from service in the Canadian forces.
But that is not an argument against the real wording of the resolution-"consideration." We have heard to-day from the hon. member for Spadina, whom I regard as the second best speaker in this house. I am not pointing to myself, because I really do not know who takes first place. I remember so well the hon. member discussing this matter last year, but, with respect, he said largely the same thing, -although he clothed it in different and more beautiful language.
There is no doubt about -the fact that a home market is the best market, but what is a home market that does not earn its living and cannot pay for the things which are produced? I know I am playing right into the hands of my hon. friends over here for a moment, but if they will follow me long enough they will find that the trail has turned and that they are still on the by-road which they have been on for a long, long time.

the many untilled acres that we have. We
had a debate in this house the other' day about untilled acres in the northern part of Alberta and British Columbia-I see the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) back there; but why are they not tilled? Because even now, with the world crying for food, we cannot till them effectively, on account of lack of transportation. This thing cannot be regarded all by itself; it must fit itself into the great puzzle-and I use that word advisedly-of our economy. I should get applause for that word from the planners to my left. After all, it is something which has been built up through changing circumstances through the lifetime of everybody in this house.
What happened under our last policy of bringing farmers into this country? They must serve on a farm for six months. How many of them are there to-day? Not five per cent of the people we brought in under that policy. I have no statistics to prove it, but in areas with which I am familiar I am perfectly certain that that percentage is fcorrect. Why will they not stay on the farms? For the reason advanced the other day in another building in which I was: that farming has not been profitable. You men in this House of Commons who come from farms and who have sons coming back from this war are having difficulty in maintaining them there. Why? It is easy to say that the farmer in Canada has been better off in the' past five years than he has ever been before. Certainly he has; there is no question about it. But the sons are not staying there because farming is not profitable.
I am going to pose a question for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), who I see has just come into the chamber; and I flatter myself it is because somebody told him I was speaking. If one looks over the history of Canada, and those of us who have been in this country for any length of time know this, it will be realized that the hard work has been done by the immigrant. The mines, the work in the brickyards, the labour on the farm, the bush labour-all that has been done by the immigrant. It is true that he grew up, got himself some cash, and as his intelligence merited or warranted he went on and did many other things. My own grandparents came to this country on the same basis. if it was not he, it should have been-helped him out by talking about the Japs; and we have also the conscientious objectors. In spite of all that we are going to have some difficulty in

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the 'advisability of instituting a reasonable immigration programme, planned in accordance with Canada's absorptive capacity, its economic needs and possibilities of development.
Experience shows that a reasonable immigration programme cannot possibly be carried out. I do not question the sincerity of the mover of this resolution. But I believe that the [DOT] time is ill-chosen even for its consideration. It is not when returned men are looking for employment and shelter that any thought should be given to opening the door to immigration, even on a moderate scale. When more than 200,000 people are unemployed, our duty is to solve that distressing problem rather than make it worse through immigration, however moderate it might be. There is no room for immigrants in Canada. Our sole duty is to put our own house in order. It would be inconceivable that we should do , otherwise; we would thus disregard our responsibilities. Let us at least show some fairness

to those who are in search of a job or a house. When our soldiers are still policing Germany, is it proper that the government should be asked to admit foreigners to this country? The most elementary justice demands that we bring our men back, up to the last one, before even thinking about immigration. Canada has first to ensure security for its own citizens. We are not in a position to absorb even a very small flow of immigrants. We must first restore our economic and social life. All our strength must be devoted to this worthy object. The economic needs of our country forbid all immigration. The reestablishment of social order is of greater import than any kind of immigration. The return to civilian life of our thousands of young men who have served in our armed forces must be undertaken with method, fairness and justice. Those whose careers have been interrupted or jeopardized by the war are entitled to assistance and protection by the government.
I now come to the third part of the resolution moved by the hon. member:
Canada's possibilities of development.
Our country is rich in natural resources. Part of them have not yet been developed. We do not need immigrants for that task. Our people are more than equal to it. The transition from the state of war to normal peacetime activities is a slow process. We are not short of experts and technicians for developing our resources. The conversion of our war industries into civilian industries would, alone, bring a solution for years to come to the problem of the development of our resources. We have the required manpower. How many heads of families and young men are receiving unemployment insurance benefits rather than the fruit of their labour which would ennoble their lives? Why should we allow immigrants to compete with our own citizens in the quest of jobs? This would be a disastrous policy. At a time when we must suppress subversive ideas and crime, which are frequently the result of idleness, I would not think of supporting any immigration policy. Let us find jobs for our own citizens first of all. That should be our chief consideration when thinking of an immigration policy. I am as much opposed to immigration as I am in favour of Canadian citizenship.

speechtext:
In rising to support this motion, may I do as my colleague did, so there may be no misunderstanding, and read the resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the

Immigration
advisability of instituting a reasonable immigration programme, planned in accordance with Canada's absorptive capacity, its economic needs and possibilities of development.
First of all may I say that to some extent I agree with my colleague who spoke on this subject a few minutes ago. While we should certainly give consideration to this matter it would not be advisable to bring in these people at this time, when we have not housing for those of our own kith and kin, and while we have the unemployment situation which now exists. May I go a step farther than he went, and say that I do not think we should have that condition prevailing to the extent that it prevails to-day. It should have been planned against. I could take some time in setting forth an argument to prove that housing is Canada's number one problem. However, I do not want to take the time at this particular moment. The same might be said of unemployment.
I do want to take some issue with the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) in his argument that we should have more agriculturists from Europe. In my opinion agriculture has suffered more than any other activity in Canada from lopsided development. May I say before going further on that point that at the time of confederation the then prime minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, predicted that Canada would have a population of twenty-five million people during the quarter of a century following confederation. We all know what has happened. Mention has been made of a pamphlet put out quite recently by a government department which indicates that now they are hoping only for a population of some fifteen million at the end of this century, fifty years hence. Certainly these are two very different views, one expressed by the government of the day following confederation; the other by the government of the present day. For the life of me I cannot conceive of a government, with conditions as we now find them throughout the world, putting out a pamphlet of the kind at this time, in view of our present position and prospects. I do not believe there is any other nation whose undeveloped resources and whose developed and potential electrical power compare with those of Canada. Therefore we cannot lightly neglect the matter of immigration. We must give serious thought and planning to it. True, the Sirois commission points out that from the period of 1896 to 1913, under a very vigorous immigration policy by the government of the day, assisted by land companies and railway companies, a tremendous expansion took place in territories of Canada. Settlement took place
Without discrimination. The territories settled grew from about 10,000,000 acres to some
70,000,000 acres in that period. And the settlement was chiefly along agricultural lines.
I have argued many times that immigration should be on a selective basis. I have said that our development has been lopsided. I think in view of that experience we should be very careful and should encourage people who are tradesmen to come to this country now.
I have pointed out the opportunities we have for development here; and in view of what has been said by the hon. member for Spadina may I make a brief reference to another article:	[DOT]
Statistics prove that for the year 1937 the family of the average industrial employee consumed agricultural products to the extent of 85409.35 annually. These figures for to-day would be considerably higher. On this basis, if we had five million heads of families employed m industry there would be an immediate home market in Canada for our present agricultural production.
I am one who thinks that in a country such as Canada, with our vast undeveloped natural resources, our very cheap electrical power and the possibility for further development ot cheap electrical' power, we must have, during the generation following the end of the war just terminated a much greater development ot peace-time industry. This would create employment for all our ex-service men and for every able-bodied Canadian willing to work. It would also necessitate an immigration policy on a selective basis for industrial development.

I am very much in favour of the resolution. Before going into my reasons for favouring it I wish to say a word about the speech of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I do not often disagree with the hon. member. I do not disagree with him now, but it did seem to me that the manner in which he made his remarks certainly left the impression-it left the impression in my mind at any rate-that since we could not have immigration now, it was not of the importance which I for one attach to it, to have now a discussion of the matter with a view to arriving at a satisfactory plan for immigration.
To my way of thinking, now that the war is over and our liberty is secure, now that we can turn our eyes inwards towards the development of this great country, there is not a single thing which is more important to the economy of Canada or to full employment than that we should have a definite policy of mass immigration.
I want to put my remarks in the strongest possible terms, because I read the other day a short pamphlet on immigration which amused me very much. Probably most members received it. It pointed out that the first objectors to immigration into Canada were the Indians, and they objected because they were afraid that one more buck would be killed by the immigrant and there would not be enough meat to go around the few thousand Indians who then inhabited the country. The article goes on to point out that there is no possible opposition to a programme of immigration except from people of the "if" and "but" school. There is no one who will get up and say, "I am opposed to immigration". That would be a ridiculous thing.

speechtext:
I must retract what I said. There are people who are prepared to advocate a ridiculous thing. I make no bones about where I stand. I stand for mass immigration,

and I mean by mass, a very great number of people, not less than 200,000 a year over a very long period.
While I entirely agree with the member for Calgary West that it would be impossible to* start immigration in the year 1846, in view of the necessity for repatriating the rest of the troops and getting a housing programme going; while I agree that it would be folly to bring people intq the country if we are to continue the present type of muddling over housing,, instead of getting after the housing problem and providing a housing policy that will take care as well of immigrants who do come into this country, I am perfectly satisfied that the plans must, be laid now.
Let me give an illustration. All hon. members will recall the events in 1942 preceding the Battle of El Alamein. There was criticism of the Churchill government over equipment available for the troops in the preceding Gazala defeat. Mr. Churchill, speaking on that subject, pointed out that the troops which had fought at El Alamein and saved Egypt were not troops sent out by the government after the defeat in the desert. They were troops sent out before that action, with the intention of going ahead to Bengazi and Tripolitania, which was eventually done. Churchill pointed out to the house that you cannot start these great movements and bring them to completion in a moment. You must make your plans long in advance. I believe he mentioned that the time taken to transport a division from Great Britain around the cape to the middle east wTas six months after the executive order to proceed had bqen received, and the plans which the government had to lay for the campaign in the western desert were taken more than six months and sometimes as long as a year before the event about which we read in the papers. Surely the same thing exactly applies to this great problem of immigration. I shall come back to that.
For a moment I wish to turn to the reason why I say we need immigration in large numbers. The hon. member who moved the resolution was a little faint-hearted. He said that immigration would probably create more employment. I am quite satisfied that it is the one way to full employment, to increasing production which can come only from an increase in the man-power of this nation.
To the north of us we have a great new frontier and, thank goodness, we are becoming conscious of it. It is the last frontier in the world. A few days ago we had a debate on the Peace River railway, the Pacific Great Eastern. From what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) said on that occasion

Immigration
it was obvious to me that such a railway cannot be built economically with the present population in that area. There is only one way to have that railway built, and everybody knows that we need it. That is to bring into the area a population which will support the railway. That applies right across the country.
If hon. members would like to know one way to full employment, I believe I can help them. As I came 'east for this session I stopped off in the mining town of Geraldton in northern Ontario. I found it a pleasant little town of twenty-five hundred people. It contained two-storey buildings and every possible modern facility. It might be of passing interest to remark that very few people in the town were over forty years of age. The town exists because of four producing mines in the immediate vicinity. These people are there because of the discovery and development of these mines. I should like to have the reaction of the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) to the existence' of this town. I am quite sure that if these 2,500 people were in Toronto, Winnipeg, or one of the other big centres in Canada, these ministers would be much more worried than they are to-day over employment. When I was in Geraldton I was shown pictures of the town as it existed twelve years ago. All that existed was one building. Now there is a town which compares favourably with the majority of the towns in my own province, and is greater in population than many.
The other day I suggested that it is the existence of such towns as Geraldton and others that makes it possible for the industrial and financial developments which we have in our big cities. I am convinced that no other thing makes this possible.
'At the moment there is tremendous activity in the mining area of Red Lake. In the course of years we shall find the same thing happening there as happened in Geraldton. This is an area which has mines in an indefinite state of development. One can get into the area at the moment only by air. I venture to prophesy that in ten years' time there will be in that area many more than 2,500 people earning a good living for themselves and, incidentally, supporting the earnings of many people in our great industrial areas.
I come now to a second reason for an immediate programme of immigration. The reason, of course, is that in the country we should have a stable internal market upon which we may rely. I wish to make two broad
generalizations in regard to this matter. I deliberately make them broad and general because this is an important broad policy which is being advocated and we should not get down to questions as to whether or not we can put two men here or three men there. It is customary to say that in Canada three out of every eight people depend on the export trade. That is advanced as an argument to keep up our export trade. I quite agree with it and often use the .'same figures myself. But at this time I wish to reverse the figures and say that in Canada five out of eight of our people depend for their livelihood on home trade. While we are doing a great deal for the export trade to look after the wants of three of the eight, granting $2 billion in export credits, I believe we should be doing something at the same time to care for the five, the greater number. We are spending $2 billion in export credits in order that people in foreign and empire countries may buy our consumer goods. I am all in favour of that, but we should also be considering the expenditure of considerable sums of money on the development in Canada of the capital goods necessary for a greater production of wealth.
I do not wish to become involved in a discussion on export trade, but at the moment we are worried about bilateralism in trade; we are worried about how we can import from Great Britain the amount of goods to balance the exports we make to her. If we do not reach some sound agreement, or if the Bretton Woods fund does not function in the way we all hope, then we have little chance of getting back any large part of the moneys that we are advancing to France, the Netherlands, the Netherlands Indies, Russia and other countries. We should spend some of our money in the development of our public facilities, which are our capital goods.
It is necessary to bring in people for three main purposes; first, for the full use of our transport system; second, for the full use of our government facilities, and third, and perhaps most important, so that we may spread taxation and thereby reduce the per capita taxation in the country.
No matter how economically we behave- and, goodness knows, this government is not behaving economically-there is no real hope of greatly reducing the per capita taxation unless we increase the number of people who are paying taxes in this country, and increase them substantially indeed. speechtext:
I am perfectly happy to leave it in this way, that whatever may be the comparison between our civil service and that of any other country, we have far too many civil servants in comparison with our total population.
I now want to come to another point, which to me is very important. We want a policy of immigration so that we may remove from' the economy of this country the greatest of all tariff barriers, the embargo on human beings.
I put it in that way because I think it is a vivid way of putting it. We have now an 
actual embargo, with very few exceptions, on the import of human beings into this country. I was most amused at the tremendous tempest in a teapot raised last session by some hon. members opposite and by the Winnipeg Free Press over the imposition of a twenty per cent duty on diesel engines. Of all the ridiculous things, Mr. Speaker, to raise such a row about, when the same goyernment at the present time maintains practically an embargo on immigration!
Finally, of course, as other hon. members *have mentioned, the questions of world peace and national defence also come into the picture. I need not go into these matters at length, because both have ben covered by the *hon. member who introduced the resolution and by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). But I believe that to enable the people of Europe to have a decent, economic standard of living and so contribute toward world peace we must relieve them of part of their surplus population. The question of national defence speaks for itself. ,1 feel sure that we shall have introduced into the house this . session estimates for our armed forces based upon the decision that has been made as to their size. No doubt this will be all we can afford, but I believe every hon, member will be forced to agree they will be entirely inadequate for any kind of defence, of the country. The only way we can get the money and the man-power to provide a suitable form' of national defence is by increasing our population.
I now want to come to a point which explains the only difference between myself and the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) who, I see, is back in the house. The Australians say they want twenty million people, and their plan calls for seventy thousand the first year and one hundred thousand a year thereafter. For some months now they have had a committee working in the United Kingdom and on the continent-I believe headed by a cabinet minister-laying their plans and indicating their desire to accept large numbers of immigrants. Australia has given the green light to immigration. What have we done? We have done nothing so far. The other day I deliberately placed a question on the order paper to find that out. I asked how many applications had been received for immigration to Canada, and I was told that no record of applicants existed. I wish to refer to a press clipping in that connection, which appeared in January of this year in the Vancouver Province. In it a returned soldier who was connected with the Maple Leaf, the Canadian army newspaper, is quoted as having said:

Immigration
Canada has done a great job of promotion over there . . . Among Belgians particularly, and among Dutch and French, there is a great desire to come to Canada, The Canadian consular office in Brussels is besieged by citizens who regard Canada as a sort of "promised land."
All servicemen met many people in Europe whom they would consider suitable to come to this country, but how in the world are we to keep those people from going to Australia or some other country unless we at least tell them now, "You have the green light, and as soon as we can make arrangements for you we will bring you in." That is what Australia did. In the pamphlet dealing with the Australian programme it is clearly stated that Australia proposes to look after the reestablishment of her veterans and her housing problem before she brings her scheme into large-scale operation, but the pamphlet also states, "But, nevertheless, all plans are being laid now." That is what I ask from this government; not that they start flooding the country this month with mass immigration, but rather that they indicate to prospective immigrants that they are going to adopt such a policy and, second, that they lay their plans and announce them as soon as possible in order that these prospective immigrants may have a choice between Australia, New Zealand and Canada and may not be forced to go to the antipodes. The government of Australia is also arranging assisted passages for veterans, and giving preference to families with young children, who they think will be the most suitable type of immigrants. I say that is right, because the greatest wealth an immigrant can bring with him is not cash in his pockets but rather his character, education and occupational skill.
When I come to the question of ccupational skill I wish to point out that all the great movements of immigration into this country in past years have been in periods of great prosperity; and in my view that prosperity has been brought about bjj this immigration. Why do people want to come to Canada? It is because here they have a greater hope for freedom than in their native countries, and also because they hope to be able to get capital assets in their new home. Our previous mass immigration movements have relied upon homestead lands and railway lands to give the immigrants that capital, and have relied also upon railway construction. In this new era we still have vast acreages of land available for immigrants, provided that we conduct irrigation schemes, and we still have some railways to develop. However, the public capital facilities most needed now are power projects, irrigation schemes and things of that kind, as well as housing; and
it is my view that the government should coordinate a mass immigration programme with the provision 'of these capital requirements, in order to allow the immigrants to catch on in the country. Comparatively speaking, it would not cost the government a very great sum of money to do that. There can be no doubt that private business would respond to the challenge and would respond to the promise that their markets would be continuously extended in the very near future.
We have in this country a great need for the development of communications and for the development of housing. I have seen an estimate that this country needs at the present time 700,000 housing units. Of course, if we brought in more people, more housing units would be required. As I have mentioned, we need irrigation and water and power supply. I have here a pamphlet of the Canadian construction association stating that the post-war projected works will total over three billion dollars.

Second, this policy should be decided and announced now so that people in this country, not only in the government but in private walks of life may know the kind of economy we may expect in the post-war years and be able to make plans and gear their businesses to the type of economy that has been decided upon by the government.
