speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whether mass immigration is a -wise policy or opposition to mass immigration is ridiculous cannot be decided as lightly as the hon. member (Mr. Merritt) has just done. Peopling a country is not like packing sardines into a tin. The question of immigration and the possibilities of our country providing a decent standard of living for a much larger population has been a matter of great concern to economists who have failed to be in agreement with one another on the matter and who have not tried to dispose of the matter as lightly as has the hon. gentleman.
I think it was quite appropriate that the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) should bring in this resolution. I may not be in agreement with all those on this side, but I think within the life of this parliament, if not during the life of this session, this country should determine its immigration policy. It is highly necessary that we know where we stand on the question. People outside Canada should know what to expect from this country.
The immigration laws have been too elastic and, if I may say so, the administration of those laws has been more or less of a hodgepodge during the last thirty years. Fortunately, the branch has been under able ministers, and under every government there have been conscientious civil servants carrying on this work, to whom I am pleased to pay a compliment, both to those who have retired as well as to those who are still in office. But the fact remains that for the last twenty-five or thirty years Canada has had no definite immigration policy and has had also very unsatisfactory immigration laws.
I do not intend to discuss all the details of the problems of immigration, but I should like to touch upon two questions that have been mentioned by some of the previous speakers. First, it has been said that Canada is empty, that Canada needs a much larger .population if we are to dispose of our surpluses or of our production, whether in agricultural fields or in industry. That brings up the argument for mass immigration which has been so ably presented by the hon. member who has just spoken but with whom I cannot agree.
There is another school of thought which contends that we should have an open door for anyone who comes from the British isles and a door kept only partly open for those who do not come from the British isles- I am opposed to that line of thinking and I intend to say a few words about it. There is another school of thought which opposes all immigration, and again I am opposed to that. It

seems that I am against everything. But the fact of the matter is, I think a happy medium could be found in the form of functional immigration, and I shall say a few words about this before I close my remarks.
Dealing with the argument of those who say that this country is empty, I think it would be interesting to note what studies have been made in the past by economists and others who have dealt with this problem. I believe statistics were quoted last session to show that Canada could have a population of 100,000,000 people or at least 80,000,000. I have tried to find1 some information on this matter, and I remembered having been in Hamilton in 1943 when- I heard Professor Dawson of McGill university discussing this question. As I could not remember all his argument I got hold of the text of his lecture. I find that people are far from agreeing with ene another as to our possible maximum population. Those who have looked into this matter seriously put their estimates much lower than those who estimate between 80,000,000 and 100,000,000. I should like to quote from Professor Dawson's work because I think he is much more eminently versed than I and many other hon. members are in this matter. Speaking on May 24, 1943, as president of the Canadian political science association, Professor Dawson said:
In recent years we have heard much about the so-called overpopulated and underpopulated countres. The crudest form in which notions of this kind are presented is in terms of number of people per square mile of land surface. By this device Canada's 2J per square mile seems to demonstrate obvious underpopulation as compared with England's 390, forgetting that this 390 involves resources not only at home but also abroad.
It must be remembered that the population of the British isles does not thrive only upon the exploitation of the land. It exists mainly through trade and commerce. This is one argument that wiU be brought up in a short time when the question of the British loan is before us, whicji loan I will approve. I say that now in order to reassure some of my hon. friends. The argument will be advanced that Britain must import from the outside considerable materials which she in turn manufactures into finished products. British shipping thereby profits by hauling these products, and' considerable capital is also made by the manufacture or treatment of these goods while in the country before they are exported to other countries as finished products. I might use the following as an example: if my hon. friend the member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne) succeeds in his negotiations, and I am told that they are about completed, we shall be able to manufacture in Canada some

Immigration
rayon or celanese. Formerly a pulp made out of British Columbia wood was sent to Britain and there converted into rayon or celanese and then brought back to Canada and sold at a considerable profit. It was just a small item in the list of raw materials processed in Great Britain, but from now on, because of the ability and initiative of the hon. member for Beauce, a factory is being organized in the city of Quebec to treat and manufacture the pulp and make the finished product here.
But I am getting away from my first argument, that Britain can support a population much greater than ours because of its highly industrialized areas and by importing goods from all parts of the world and manufacturing them in Britain into finished products, thereby giving work to a very much larger population than its own resources alone would permit.
Those who base Canada's possible population on her area, on the surface of land, fail to take into account the actual conditions within the country. We seem to be on safer ground, when we follow Professor Dawson and take the arable land surface as a base for presenting population densities.
I have often said that instead of having a nice red map of Canada in our school books we should show, in white, what parts of this country are covered with ice and snow and are not occupied and cannot be lived in except perhaps by a musk-ox expedition. Then we should show, in a light colour, perhaps in pink, -I did not say rose-the areas which can be inhabited part of the year, and finally show in a stronger shade those parts where there is arable land.
But to come back to Professor Dawson, if we figure out our population according to the arable land surface, we see that Canada is not so vacant because we have 121 people per square mile of arable land, which is vastly different from the figures that are used by some people who say that we could have a population equal to that of the United States, if not larger. Professor Dawson says:
The arable land index should be supplemented by indices of available minerals, and closely allied items.
And so on. Nevertheless that would not warrant Canada in having such a large population as some people advocate. Professor Dawson says:
In supporting this point of view

The point of view that Canada is an empty country.
-the great mass of Canadians believe that Canada is a country of boundless resources, meagrely developed and offering great opportunities for population expansion, not only by way of natural increase at home but by immigration from abroad. Our school books have built this picture into our minds. Publicists keep inflating this conception throughout our adult years.
I might in passing remind the hon. gentleman who just spoke that with sound economic conditions within the country in past years we would not have needed immigration to have a population as large as Canada has to-day. Canada could have reached her present size of population, given sound economic conditions, without immigration, just by the natural increase in population if it had not suffered from emigration. Without the policy of forced immigration which was started forty or fifty years ago, given good economic conditions, and no emigration, Canada would have been able to reach her present population by natural increase alone, and therefore I gather that the main point that we should have under consideration is that of having a government in this country that will give to Canada as good administration as we have had in the last ten years-that is the political note in this, Mr. Speaker. Let us give the people decent standards of living which will prevent them from drifting over the boundary into the United States. By doing that we shall have, through the natural increase in population, as large a population by 1980 as Canada can sustain with a standard of living comparable to that of the United States.
Economically and geographically Canada and the United States are so vastly different that we cannot compare them simply by surface area. But we must take into account also the climate and those innumerable other factors which economists consider before arriving at their conclusions. It is all very well to speak of mass immigration, but we must also consider the productivity of which the country is capable, what parts of the country are climatically habitable, and what parts of the country we can develop with a chance of providing a decent living for our people. We have to consider so much more than is taken into account by those who simply look at the map and our surface area and say that we need a vast population to provide markets for our products. But first of all, people must have productive and remunerative work. They must have land which they can till or industries where they can be employed. Let us agree that Canada needs a larger population than she now has. But we do not need mass immigration, as some hon. gentlemen on the other side are advocating. Far from it.
Immigration

Professor Dawson in his conclusions is quite conservative. Others are a little more optimistic.. Professor Dawson says:
The shock of disillusionment enters Canadian minds when someone points out that in terms of its population possibilities Canada, like Australia, is a relatively small country and not as big as the United States. The Canadian shield and other non-arable mountainous areas comprise most of Canada. The remaining land surface is roughly 1,000,000 square miles, of which approximately 550,000 square miles is available for potential agricultural settlement, much of it very problematical. Less than one-half of this is now occupied. These latter figures give a clue to Canada's size in terms of potential settlement.
As I said before, one must not simply look at the map, because these other factors have to be taken into consideration. Professor Dawson goes on:
The pressure of the forces of nature against the settlement process in Canada is further indicated by the fact that we have been able to absorb only a portion of those available.
For the past two decades the prairie region has become an area of emigration rather than immigration. There will be some further expansion in farm acreage, but this will take place more slowly and with greater difficulty.
Now, for my friends of the prairies, Professor Dawson has this advice:
This expansion will offer a limited opportunity even for those who live on the prairies.
The development is not illimitable. There are limits to the development, of the prairies, and those who have made a thorough study of the question have realized it. Professor Waines, in his study called "Prairie Population Possibilities," which has been published under the auspices of the Rowell-Sirois commission, has this to say:
The material presented in this review affords no basis for the belief that the presently unexploited resources of the prairie provinces are capable of supporting large additions to the present population. Assuming a continuance of present factors it appears that the prairie provinces will not find it easy in the early future to support their own natural increase, and that any attempt to enhance the population by assisted immigration or land settlement schemes will probably merely accentuate to that degree the present emigration.
That is not my statement; it is from a professor who was considered versed enough or enlightened enough on such questions to be called by the Rowell-Sirois commission to prepare a study for their consideration on that matter.' To go back to Professor Dawson, I might add this statement of his:
In terms of our climate, resources and competitive location, the evidence points against any marked expansion of occupational opportunities.

Which is another thing to be considered.
Indeed we may be pushed to the limit to give-chances for livelihood to our present population as augmented by natural increase.
I have considered this question objectively, as has been my habit through life, to try to-find out the facts. I had no preconceived ideas. I do not get them from any newspaper, whether in my city or province or elsewhere. I just want to try to have an opinion of my own on the question. I have tried to find the arguments on both sides. When I was with the late Mr. Lapointe I was fortunate in that he received a great deal of information on immigration from all kinds of immigration societies, and I retained it for my own use when the files were disposed of. Some expressed very eloquently the belief that we should be the second British empire, the heart of the British empire, and bring all the British isles over here-which might be easy to do geographically but not so practical ethnically. My mind has been much more satisfied on this question by the studies of Professor Dawson, as well as those of Professor Forsey, from which I shall quote in a moment. Frankly, I believe that no hon. member should approach this question with a biased mind. There are some, in my province and elsewhere, who say that we do not want anybody; that we are satisfied to be alone: there are others who say, let us open the doors to our friends on condition they are of our own racial stock. My opinion is different, and I shall give it as I conclude my remarks. But I beg every hon. member, when he considers this question, whether he is now inclined to one side or the other, to open his mind to arguments from the other side, and then to try to find where lies the happy medium for our country. I do not think the solution is to be found in mass immigration; I do not think it is to be found through the closed door. There is bound to be a happy medium.
Professor Dawson is more conservative than anybody else. He has devoted many years, he says, to incidental studies of the question; that is, he has not spent many years in an exclusive study of it but has given quite a lengthy period of time throughout his life to incidental studies of the matter, and he comes to a conclusion which, to me, seems a bit pessimistic, that Canada could, give a standard of living comparable to that of the United States to a population of only eighteen million people. As I say, I think that may be pessimistic, although the man is much better versed in economy than I can be. Professor Forsey is inclined to go to a limit of thirty million; yet he himself admits that

Immigration
that may be stretching the possibilities of . the country. He says that it cannot be foreseen, that it depends on the development of economic trends throughout the world, and on many other factors on which the figures cannot be available, and on problems of which he cannot foresee the solution, but he thinks the most optimistic appraisal could reach that figure. That might be put into the possession of those who, when they go back to Britain, and sit on commissions to investigate conditions in Canada, come to conclusions somewhat like that Australian professor who used to say that we could have on our eastern shores about one hundred million people, or, including the eastern shores of the United States and Canada, about
130,000,000 in that part alone. Such fantastic figures cannot be supported by anybody. The most conservative figure is 18,000,000. The most optimistic implies, as Professor Forsey says, the possibility of extending our arable lands farther to the north, climatic changes, and improvements in the possibilities of inhabiting cold climates, as have been attempted in Siberia and certain parts of Russia. But taking all these things into account, and trying to be fair to those who believe that Canada can maintain a huge population, he concludes that we cannot reach a figure higher than I have mentioned. As Professor Forsey says:
It is not a question of how many human beings can squash into a particular territory, nor even of how much that territory can physically be made to produce, cost what it may, it is a question of costs and markets.
It is not a question of sending people there and saying, we will put them there even if it means a loss; we must have people ,in that part of the country. If we want to have in Canada a sound economy we must make sure that the people who are located anywhere will produce at a' marked advantage to the [DOT]economy of the country in general. Professor Forsey says:
We might, for example, divide the nine million acres of unoccupied "agricultural" land in "the northwest territories into 56,250 farms of 160 acres each, and we might succeed in growing a crop on them. But how much would it *cost? And where could we sell it, and at what price? Of the already occupied farm land in Canada only about 38-5 per cent is actually in use.
That refers to the amount which is occupied. Maybe only half of the potential arable land is occupied, but even where it may be usable from a climatic point of view, much of the land does not lend itself to cultivation with profit, because the geographic conditions are
such that the land cannot be profitably operated. It is not worth while to cultivate it because, says Professor Forsey:
. . . the produce costs too much to grow; because markets are too restricted or too far away, or both; because of European and American tariffs, quotas and embargoes.
It is admitted by everybody that the farmer can no longer live directly off his land except at an exceedingly low standard of living. On the pre-depression standards of western Canada, says Professor Dawson, he had to buy two-thirds of his living necessities. No civilized man could be expected to obtain all his wants out of the products of nature.
These are the aspects of the argument which have convinced me that geographically Canada cannot accept a vast immigration scheme, having regard to its natural growth, as we have seen it in the past. As I said before, had there been no emigration from Canada, and no forced immigration, our population to-day would be exactly what it is. Let us give the country a sound economical administration and we shall retain the people we have without being under the necessity of bringing in
200,000	a year, as someone suggested.
There is another point. Some people say that we should throw our doors open to immigration from the British isles. I have no prejudice at all against anyone from the British isles. I have visited Great Britain quite often and have been well received there, and I have admired the qualities of the British people, not only as empire builders but in many other ways. Although I am of French descent, I do not mind saying that on one occasion a scene I witnessed brought tears to my eyes. I see some of my hon. friends smiling, but that was my reaction to the union jack. I was cruising on the Adriatic and our ship was supposed to enter the Bay of Kotor in Jugoslavia. We were told that we had to be up by 5.30 a.m., and though that was not in keeping with my habits, I did get up. As the sun was dispersing the mists of the morning we saw sombre masses on the water not very far from our cruise ship, and we heard a bugle call. Presently a flag was hoisted and it was the union jack. The whole Mediterranean fleet was at anchor in that vast bay. I was surrounded by Americans, and, though it may sound queer to some hon. gentlemen, I did have a feeling of pride at the thought that I was a British subject.
I take people exactly as I find them for what they are, and when it comes to immigration I consider them from the point of view of what they can give the country. I cannot believe that opening our doors wide to any-
Immigration

one who is British is necessarily the best thing for Canada, and in the few minutes left to me I shall illustrate my view on this point. In my opinion we should consider immigration in relation to certain groups which I shall enumerate.
The first group, comprising people who are
educated and who at the same time have money, will prefer to stay at home. Those who have established businesses and business connections will normally -remain in their own country rather than come to Canada. We might have some people from other European countries who, having suffered as they have done, are willing to take whatever capital they have left and come here and buy land, or establish a business in Canada. Anyone in Britain who is well off will not, however, come to Canada merely for the" sake of helping us.
The second group will comprise those people who have a little capital and who desire to emigrate. Such people will do as they did before the war. They will go to India, if they are still welcome there, or they will go to Burma, where cheap labour costs have in the past produced substantial profits. Those people, having a little money, will invest it where it will bring them the greatest financial returns and they will not come here simply to increase the population of Canada or to provide more profits here. People in the British isles who have capital and who are willing to come could be the preferred ones; I grant even that to you, but we should not exclude people from other countries who also have capital and who are willing to invest it here. But there should be no hide-and-seek capital as there was at one time to circumvent our immigration laws. At that time someone would deposit $1,000 in a bank in Canada in the name of So-and-so, some prospective immigrant, who would come into the country, and after that capital had remained in the bank for a few months, it was transferred back to the society overseas and deposited again in the name of someone else, another immigrant, to enable that person to come into the country. That applied, of course, to nomBritish because the same condition was not demanded of people from the British isles. But that practice was carried on extensively.
I would be willing to give priority but not exclusivity to people from the British isles who wish to bring in their capital and settle here, but I do not believe that many would come. I believe that they would rather stay at home. I do not blame them; they have a beautiful country and naturally they prefer to stay there.

In the third group there are those people who have had a fairly good education but who are not technicians or specialists. They are not people who have business connections. They prefer England, but they are willing to make sacrifices'in order to go to some other country, provided that conditions are acceptable. I met one such person on the train not long ago. He said to me, "You should hold out some inducement to us. We are somebody and we should be sure of having jobs when we come here, instead of being left at the caprice, at the mercy of someone in Canada. We are somebody, and the moment we come in we should be given special treatment."
Well, in my opinion they are no better than the people our universities turn out from Halifax to Vancouver. They are not specialists, but ordinary, well-educated people, and we have many such people in Canada who are quite capable of filling the jobs that are available. We should not throw our doors open to those people. They are no better than our people because they come from the British isles. I have said to such people, "The Canadian Pacific Railway company, the Canadian National and many large corporations, and even -the civil service of Canada have given you enough preference in the past, but that should not be extended indefinitely except in the case of experts and technicians."
We have to develop the countiy, but at the same, time we must see that our people have a decent standard of living. The people we need are experts and technicians, not simply clerks. Those we can find in our own schools. This person with whom I had the conversation on the train also said to me, "In order to induce us to face the rigours of your climate and to adapt ourselves to your way of life you should give us some special consideration." I do not agree with this. In Ontario, in Quebec and in the west there are many young men from our schools who are quite capable of managing our companies or of being clerks. We do not need to get such people from outside.
The fourth group comprises skilled labourers of whom there is a scarcity. We have a scarcity of certain technicians. I am in favour of bringing in such people either from the British isles or from the continent, because we need leather chemists, glass experts, textile experts and so on. We should open our doors to them without too many restrictions. It would be for the good of the country.
I would not close the door to anyone who could be useful and help to make Canada a

Immigration
greater country. Far from it. This group of people, whether from the British isles or from the continent, should be allowed to come in.
I do not mind having them come from the British isles if they qualify.
The fifth group is that of unskilled labourers,' unemployed persons or persons who were on the dole before they went into the army in England. They are not adaptable to Canada and they are not the people we need-at any rate until our conditions are sufficiently stabilized and we know that we can go through the after-war period without a depression and without any lowering of our productive capacity. We must make sure that we can provide work for our own population and maintain our own standard of living. If this is not assured, we must not extend our facilities to others.
I am opposed to mass immigration of this type of people. Let me illustrate this with an incident that was related to me by a former minister of the crown who is now sitting on a commission. He told me he had a large farm in the west. At the time we had opened our doors to unemployed miners from Wales or elsewhere who had not worked for a long time. They came on his farm and he said to me: "We were asking our people to get up early and work all day, to eat as much as they could. We had wagons on the farm with beans and everything they wanted to eat. They could eat ten times a day, but they had to work from sunup to sundown." He said, "After a day or two these people said, 'What about union hours?'" They did not want to work from sunup to sundown. They were not used to 'that. They were fed up with the condition and he was fed up with them, and most of these people drifted back to Winnipeg and other cities, and finally clogged the labour market. Some of them were not much of an asset to the country and many of them had to be repatriated overseas. I do not think that type of people can be of much use to Canada at the moment. I am still amazed if that is what is proposed by some people.
We have now come to the point where conclusions should be arrived at. If Canada had functional immigration, that is immigration of people who would1 become an asset to the country, it would be all to the good. We cannot foresee how future generations may turn out. They may turn out to be bad citizens, but we can at least make sure that the first generation which comes in will be useful.
I would welcome to Canada, as I indicated in my remarks, first the people with capital who wish to buy land or to establish a business
in Canada. We need the type of people who can provide capital, and they should be welcomed regardless of the part of the world from which they eome. The second class is specialists. We need them. There the advice of experts in economy and in the labour movement could be obtained. We should determine that and have quotas. Specialists, technicians, scientists, physicians, engineers and highly-trained people should be welcomed to Canada. We have need for them in many fields of endeavour. Skilled labourers may be a great asset to the country.
I would limit the people who come in just because they have a relative in the country. At the moment I believe the law is that wives and unmarried children under eighteen years of age joining family heads already established in Canada may be admitted. That is all right, and I agree with it, but I think in the past the policy has been to extend it to the seventh cousin on both sides. That permits a lot of people to come in because one man is already in Canada. Many of these people may not be of the same high standard as the one who has already arrived in Canada.
I looked up the regulations as they existed a few years ago and they would appear to be all right. It mentioned wives and unmarried children, father and mother. I would even include brothers and sisters if they can qualify. They should be given preferred treatment, but it should1 not extend to the seventh cousin as has been done in the past.
Formerly farmers bringing capital sufficient to establish them on the land were admitted, but we should demand guarantees from these people. There should not be a transfer of money from one person to another and the land held nominally in the name of So-and-so to permit them to get in, and then the land sold within three months with the result that Joe ends up in Winnipeg, Montreal or some other city and the land passes to the association and another man enters on that land. We must have some security to make sure that the man who comes to settle on the land intends to settle on the land and does not w>ant to enter another business in Montreal, Vancouver or Winnipeg.
I am against both extremes in this matter, whether they come from my province or my party or elsewhere, or from any particular group which says, "let us not open the door; let us keep it closed; it is dangerous_ to Canada." We need new people in limited number provided that they can be useful. I am against mass immigration of people without taking into consideration the, service that they may render to the country. I am in favour of some immigration, not because
Immigration

they will eat our food, but because they can produce something without taking the place of some of our workers, because they can occupy land which can be cultivated; not just to bring them in for the sake of packing sardines in a tin. Let us allow these people to come in who may be an asset to Canada, and let us keep the others out whatever their racial origin may be.
I think this was an opportune time for the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) to bring this problem to the attention of the government and of the house. We must have the courage to face this matter within the life of this parliament. I am not in a hurry as other hon. members may be and say that it must be done this year. Because of the opinions I have expressed I do not believe there is any hurry about it. Within a reasonable time we must have the courage to face the situation and to formulate an immigration policy so that the population may know where it stands as far as the expansion of the country is concerned and that people in other lands may know what they can expect from us. This problem should be tackled within a reasonable tirpe. Let us do it within the life of this parliament.

I wish to take about two or three minutes of the time of thp house to discuss this question. In my six months in the House of Commons I have already spoken three times on this subject.
I feel that there has been enough said to-day and on other occasions thoroughly to convince the members of the house that immigration is one of Canada's most pressing problems at the present time. I can see only three possible solutions for the government to take. The first is to do nothing as has been done over the past few years. The second is to announce a quota which will permit people from other countries to come to Canada., I say that becausa lack of knowledge of what the government intends to do is causing real hardship in the country, read hardship amongst those Canadians who are interested in bringing their relatives and loved ones here. As I see it, the third solution is immediately to set up a committee on this problem, study the various aspects of it and bring down a report this session, if possible.
I was one of those who curtailed his remarks last session because I understood that a committee had' been promised and would be set up this session. So far, we have had no announcement from the minister on this subject. In fairness to hon. members, who like me, understood that there would be a committee this session, the government should make some announcement on this subject.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PLANNED IN RELATION TO ABSORPTIVE CAPACITY, ECONOMIC NEED AND DEVELOPMENT POSSIBILITIES
speechtext:
When we review the history of immigration before, during and after the war as set out in the splendid bluebook of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) it will be found that something should be done first of all for Great Britain. What Great Britain' suffered in the war and is suffering' to-day is something that should be considered, particularly with regard to those who wish to come to this country. I urge on the government that we should have a forward, courageous immigration policy adapted to Canada's circumstances. I do not mean by this that we should interfere with the employment of our own people who have been overseas, and others, but the time has come for a forward policy on immigration to let the empire know what our policy is for the three main problems of empire trade, defence and immigration within the empire, especially the latter.
After all the British people have suffered, surely we should take some steps along the lines taken by New Zealand and Australia on assisted passages for them and come at once to some agreement with them in connection with immigration adapted to our circumstances. I believe some consideration should also be given to some of those French soldiers who were on the side of the allies during the war. However, until such time as conditions improve, I believe immigration from the continent of Europe should be largely restricted for a short period of time, though in my opinion we should have in the first primary class assisted passages and other forms of assisted immigration from the British isles, though not to interfere with absorption in employment for our own soldiers and citizens.
I believe those are the three cardinal principles that should be laid down. I do not want to see the unrestricted emigration we had after the last war and between the two wars, when nearly 1,250,000 unemployed people left Canada for the United States because they could not find employment here. Those figures were given in a return tabled in the house, and they included many thousands of Canadian soldiers who had fought for their country at the hazard of their lives. Where did they go? They went mainly to the United States, owing to conditions here resulting from the trade and other policies of the government.
In conclusion, I urge upon the minister that we should decide something right away This is a very important question. First comes migration within the empire. What is

Labour Conditions
to be done to help those who assisted us during the war? I believe British immigration should come first; then migration within the empire; in the next place we have a large number coming from the United States who must be considered. Then the continent of Europe, with priority for our allies there, must be considered. In my opinion we should not bring refugees here from Europe only to become a charge on the municipalities, as happened after the last war. Let us carefully consider this matter and send them aid. I was the head of a municipality at that time, and I can tell you that refugees were brought from all parts of the world, with the result that some of them became a charge on the taxpayers of our cities and towns and on real estate. I have great sympathy for the refugees and their suffering, but I believe there are conditions within our own empire which should receive prior consideration. So that I think the time has come when the government should not be afraid to tell the people of Canada and the people of the empire what their policy is, and adopt a forward policy like those of Australia and New Zealand, for if we do not come to some agreement in connection with immigration all these people will go to Australia and New Zealand. Many people in Britain desiring to come to Canada are key men who are badly needed in various skilled, industries in this dominion. I am sure many industries will be very glad to get people of this kind, many of whom they cannot get in this country, and so aid reconversion and production. Therefore I urge upon the minister that some definite action should be taken almost immediately, and a government plan announced at once, so that the house and the country may know what it is.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this resolution may I say that the discussion to-day has been particularly gratifying to me because I believe I was the first to raise the question of our immigration policy in this parliament. No doubt this matter has been discussed on previous occasions, but I brought it up in the house last September, and again a little later on. The expressions of opinion we have heard from all sides to-day have been very helpful. Whatever may be the ultimate fate of the resolution, I believe the discussion will show that all parties in this house are interested in this most important question, and it will give the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) an opportunity to place before the house his opinions and whatever plans may be ready.
I believe the question of immigration can be divided into two main categories. First there is the long-range policy, which has been particularly discussed up to the present, and then the immediate policy.
On motion of Mr. Zaplitny the debate was adjourned.
